extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners subject to USPTO disciplinary rules (practitioners before the USPTO), USPTO OED staff, and counsel handling reciprocal discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and defenses for imposing identical reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 based on a State disciplinary suspension; explains the elements a respondent must rebut and the Director's remedial powers. Useful for attorneys facing reciprocal discipline or counsel briefing such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of reciprocal discipline (Selling/37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: State disbarment/suspension creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper under Selling v. Radford and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Director 'shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact' as to one of the listed defenses. Federal review is narrow; the Director is not sitting as a court of review to find errors in the state proceedings. The practitioner bears the burden to rebut the presumption by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process" (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that the state disciplinary procedure deprived the respondent of due process (i.e., lacked notice or opportunity to be heard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires meaningful opportunity to be heard (Mathews v. Eldridge). In disciplinary proceedings this includes reasonable notice of charges and opportunities to present evidence, testify, cross-examine, and be represented by counsel. Mere disagreement with discovery rulings or routine procedural rulings does not establish denial of due process; the respondent must show deprivation of meaningful participation (cases: In re Karlen, In re Squire, Ruffalo). Evidence of active participation (motions filed, multi-day trial, pretrial conferences, testimony) weighs against a due-process deprivation claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: "There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject" (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that the state decision rests on such deficient evidence that the USPTO cannot accept the state finding as final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The respondent must show more than disagreement with how the factfinder weighed evidence; must demonstrate 'such an infirmity of proof' as to give rise to a clear conviction that the Office could not accept the conclusion. This is a difficult showing (see In re Zdravkovich). Challenges that exhibits were unauthenticated or that no live witnesses testified must contend with the record (e.g., stipulations to authenticity/admissibility are dispositive). The burden is clear and convincing proof of a genuine issue of material fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The imposition of the same public censure...suspension...would result in a grave injustice" (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that imposing identical discipline would produce a grave injustice—i.e., the punishment is so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that it would be unjust to impose it again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grave-injustice review focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct and allows consideration of mitigating factors and precedent. Courts/Boards evaluate whether the state sanction falls within the state's allowable range of penalties and whether the state decision is contrary to fairly uniform precedent. If the sanction is within the state's normal range and consistent with precedent, grave injustice is unlikely to be found (citations: In re Thav; In re Kramer; In re Benjamin). Speculative allegations (retaliation/collusion) without documentary proof will not meet the clear-and-convincing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified" (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense premised on the claim that the practitioner was not in fact publicly disciplined in the manner asserted by the state order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director considers timely-filed responses contesting whether the state imposed public discipline. Documentary proof in the state record controls. If the state order in fact imposed the listed discipline, the USPTO will generally impose the identical discipline absent a successful showing under (i)-(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for defeating reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent must 'clearly and convincingly demonstrate' a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the defenses in § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts (and the USPTO) treat this as a narrow standard; the respondent carries the burden of proof. Precedent (In re Kramer; In re Friedman) recognizes the difficulty of overturning state disciplinary findings in reciprocal proceedings. Evidence must be persuasive and go beyond mere assertions or speculative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process components in disciplinary-review analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes meaningful participation and procedural fairness in the underlying state disciplinary process (factors the Director examines when considering a due-process defense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key components: reasonable notice of charges; opportunity to present evidence and witnesses; opportunity to testify and rebut; opportunity to cross-examine (if the opposing party calls witnesses); representation by counsel; access to pretrial procedures and appeals within the state process. The Director will look to the state record (motions, pretrial conferences, multi‑day hearings, transcripts) to determine whether these elements were provided. Absence of opposing witnesses to cross-examine does not show deprivation if the respondent nonetheless had opportunity to present rebuttal evidence and witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary effect of stipulations to authenticity/admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's stipulation to the authenticity or admissibility of exhibits in the state record limits later attacks on those exhibits in the reciprocal-review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state record shows the respondent stipulated to exhibit authenticity or admissibility, the USPTO Director will rely on that stipulation; arguments that exhibits were unauthenticated or hearsay will fail absent a record-based showing to the contrary. Challenges to the evidentiary basis must be specific and part of the state record to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of sanction / 'fit' and range-of-penalties analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment whether the state-imposed sanction falls within the normal and allowable range for the misconduct, and whether it is consistent with precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review examines the state's rules governing sanctions (e.g., Michigan Rule 9.106) and whether the state's adjudicative body considered mitigating/aggravating factors and precedent. The state board will not disturb a panel's sanction unless it is clearly outside the range of sanctions for similar misconduct. If the sanction is within that range and consistent with precedent, reciprocal imposition is generally appropriate and does not constitute grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for USPTO reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline before the USPTO is predicated on the practitioner having been suspended/disciplined by a duly constituted state authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline is not dependent on an independent OED investigation of the underlying misconduct; it is triggered by a state discipline order. The timing question (whether the misconduct occurred before the USPTO Rules' effective date) is generally resolved by reference to the date of the state discipline order; if the state suspended the attorney after the USPTO Rules were effective, reciprocal discipline may be imposed even if the underlying misconduct occurred earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner status and USPTO jurisdiction (definition of 'practitioner')
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is subject to USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction: individuals authorized to practice before the Office in trademark or other non-patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under § 11.1 and § 11.19(a), 'practitioner' includes individuals authorized under 5 U.S.C. 500(b) or § 11.14 to practice before the Office in trademark/non-patent matters. Evidence such as an attorney's admission that they are attorney of record on pending USPTO applications supports subject-matter jurisdiction; once a person meets the practitioner definition, they are subject to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and disciplinary jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible disciplinary orders and remedial measures upon reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies the USPTO Director may impose when reciprocal discipline is appropriate (types of identical discipline and ancillary orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director shall impose the identical public censure/public reprimand/probation/disbarment/suspension/disciplinary disqualification. Ancillary measures may include publication of a Notice in the Official Gazette, notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts, dissociation of the respondent's name from USPTO Customer Numbers and PKI certificates, prohibiting application for or association with Customer Numbers until reinstatement, and public availability of disciplinary records (e.g., OED Reading Room / FOIA).
